content: Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas that presents with abdominal pain and elevated pancreatic enzyme levels in the blood. It can be associated with various underlying conditions and, depending on its severity, may lead to significant complications and high mortality rates despite medical intervention. The first clinical description of acute pancreatitis was provided by Nicholas Tulp, a Dutch anatomist, in 1652. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, researchers such as Reginald Fitz, Nicholas Senn, and Eugene Opie made significant contributions to the understanding of this condition. In 1901, Eugene Opie proposed the duct obstruction hypothesis, suggesting that obstruction of the pancreatic duct impairs pancreatic outflow, leading to pancreatitis. Later that same year, he introduced the common channel hypothesis, which posited that an impacted gallstone at the papilla of Vater creates a shared channel between the pancreatic and bile ducts, allowing bile to flow into the pancreatic duct and trigger pancreatitis. In 1963, the first Marseilles Symposium introduced a clinicopathologic classification of pancreatitis, which was revised in 1984 during the second Marseilles Symposium. Finally, in 1992, the Atlanta Symposium established a clinically based classification system for acute pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis is classified into three categories: 1. Mild acute pancreatitis: Characterized by the absence of organ failure and local or systemic complications. 2. Moderately severe acute pancreatitis: Defined by transient organ failure (lasting less than 48 hours) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure. 3. Severe acute pancreatitis: Marked by persistent organ failure involving one or more organs for more than 48 hours. The pathophysiology of acute pancreatitis involves the disruption of intracellular and extracellular compartmentation, obstruction of pancreatic secretory transport, and activation of pancreatic enzymes. Once the disease begins, interstitial edema and inflammatory infiltration are key features. The accumulation of polymorphonuclear granulocytes in pancreatic and extrapancreatic tissues, along with the release of leukocyte enzymes, plays a critical role in disease progression and the development of systemic complications. There are numerous causes of acute pancreatitis, including: Gallstones: The most common cause, accounting for 40–70% of cases. Alcohol consumption: Responsible for 25–35% of cases in the United States. Hypertriglyceridemia: Serum triglyceride levels exceeding 1000 mg/dL (11 mmol/L) can precipitate acute pancreatitis, though lower levels may also contribute. This accounts for 1–14% of cases. Post-ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography): Acute pancreatitis occurs in approximately 3% of diagnostic ERCP cases, 5% of therapeutic ERCP cases, and up to 25% of sphincter of Oddi manometric studies. Genetic predisposition: Patients with genetic risk factors may experience recurrent acute pancreatitis or childhood-onset pancreatitis without an identifiable cause, which may progress to chronic pancreatitis. Medications: Drug-induced pancreatitis is rare, with a generally excellent prognosis and low mortality. Infections and toxins: Various infectious agents have been implicated, including: Viruses: Mumps, coxsackievirus, hepatitis B, cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster, herpes simplex, and HIV. Bacteria: Mycoplasma, Legionella, Leptospira, and Salmonella. Fungi: Aspergillus. Parasites: Toxoplasma, Cryptosporidium, and Ascaris. Other rare causes: These include biliary sludge, microlithiasis, biliary obstruction, and hypercalcemia. Differentiating acute pancreatitis from other conditions that cause epigastric abdominal pain is essential. Clinical features and laboratory studies help distinguish it from other diseases, such as: Peptic ulcer disease: Typically presents with intermittent epigastric pain that does not radiate to the back. Choledocholithiasis or cholangitis: Patients often have a history of gallstones or prior biliary procedures, such as ERCP. Cholecystitis: Characterized by right upper quadrant or epigastric pain that may radiate to the right shoulder or back. Perforated viscus: Presents with sudden-onset abdominal pain, peritoneal signs (guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness), and is not associated with acute pancreatitis. Intestinal obstruction: Features include abdominal pain, anorexia, vomiting, obstipation or constipation, and elevated serum amylase and lipase levels.
